# 1. Learning Outcome

This exercise measures how easy it is to reach eldercare services across Singapore. I compute accessibility on a grid of 250m hexagons using three methods, Hansen's potential model, KD2SFCA and the Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM), then map each result and compare the scores by URA planning region.

Along the way I practise importing polygon and point data with **sf**, importing an aspatial distance matrix, reshaping it into the form the modelling package expects, and visualising the output with **tmap** and **ggplot2**.

# 2. The Data

Four data sets are used:

- `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL`: URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundaries, from data.gov.sg.
- `hexagons`: a 250m radius hexagon grid made with `st_make_grid()` of sf, in ESRI shapefile format. Each hexagon is a demand point.
- `ELDERCARE`: locations of eldercare services, from data.gov.sg, in ESRI shapefile format. Each centre is a supply point.
- `OD_Matrix`: a distance matrix in csv format with six fields:
  - `origin_id`: the `fid` of the hexagon.
  - `destination_id`: the `fid` of the eldercare centre.
  - `entry_cost`: the perpendicular distance between the origin and the nearest road.
  - `network_cost`: the network distance between origin and destination.
  - `exit_cost`: the perpendicular distance between the destination and the nearest road.
  - `total_cost`: the sum of the three costs above.

All cost fields are in metres. Apart from the URA subzone data, the other three data sets were prepared by Prof. Kam for teaching and research, so they stay within this course unless he approves otherwise.

# 3. Installing and Loading the R Packages

The packages for this exercise:

- **sf** for importing and handling geospatial data.
- **SpatialAcc** for the accessibility models.
- **tidyverse**, mainly readr and dplyr, for attribute data handling. It also brings in ggplot2, tidyr and others.
- **tmap** for thematic maps.
- **ggstatsplot** for statistical graphics and analysis.
- **reshape2**, which the reference loads alongside the others.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(tmap, SpatialAcc, sf,
               ggstatsplot, reshape2,
               tidyverse)
```

`ggstatsplot` is not called in the main walkthrough but gets a use in the Extras.

# 4. Geospatial Data Wrangling

## 4.1 Importing geospatial data

The three shapefiles sit in `data/geospatial`. `st_read()` of sf takes the folder as `dsn` and the file name as `layer`.

```{r}
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")
hexagons <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "hexagons")
eldercare <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "ELDERCARE")
```

`mpsz` comes in as a multipolygon simple feature object. The reference says it has no EPSG information, so I checked the EPSG slot of all three layers instead of only the first.

```{r}
sapply(list(mpsz = mpsz, hexagons = hexagons, eldercare = eldercare),
       function(x) st_crs(x)$epsg)
```

An `NA` here means GDAL read the `.prj` file but could not match it to an EPSG code. The three `.prj` files do not name the CRS the same way: `mpsz` is labelled `SVY21`, while `hexagons` and `eldercare` are labelled `SVY21_Singapore_TM`. That alone could explain why they are not all treated alike.

## 4.2 Updating CRS information

All three layers are set to the SVY21 code, EPSG 3414.

```{r}
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414)
hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414)
```

Checking `mpsz` with `st_crs()`:

```{r}
st_crs(mpsz)
```

The ID line at the bottom should now read EPSG 3414. Repeating the earlier EPSG check across the three layers:

```{r}
sapply(list(mpsz = mpsz, hexagons = hexagons, eldercare = eldercare),
       function(x) st_crs(x)$epsg)
```

## 4.3 Cleaning and updating attribute fields

`eldercare` and `hexagons` carry many redundant fields. I keep only what is needed and add a `capacity` field to `eldercare` and a `demand` field to `hexagons` with `mutate()` of dplyr.

```{r}
eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)
```

```{r}
hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)
```

Both values are a constant 100, which is a teaching placeholder. A real analysis would use actual demand for each hexagon and actual capacity for each centre.

One thing about `eldercare` before moving on. The accessibility function matches centres to distance-matrix columns by position, so the IDs matter.

```{r}
nrow(eldercare)
range(eldercare$fid)
```

There are 120 centres, yet `fid` runs from 1 to 133, so 13 ids are missing. Section 5.2 checks that the distance matrix skips the same ids.

# 5. Aspatial Data Handling and Wrangling

## 5.1 Importing the distance matrix

`read_csv()` of readr brings `OD_Matrix.csv` in as a tibble called `ODMatrix`.

```{r}
#| message: false
ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)
```

```{r}
head(ODMatrix)
```

The matrix is stored in long form: one row per origin and destination pair. With 3,125 hexagons and 120 centres, that should come to 375,000 rows.

```{r}
dim(ODMatrix)
```

## 5.2 Tidying the distance matrix

Most modelling packages in R expect a wide matrix. Rows are origins (the `from` field) and columns are destinations (the `to` field). `spread()` of tidyr turns the thin table into a fat one.

```{r}
distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  spread(destination_id, total_cost)%>%
  select(c(-c('origin_id')))
```

```{r}
dim(distmat)
```

Since tidyr 1.0, `pivot_wider()` is the recommended function and `spread()` is retired. `spread()` still runs here, so I kept it as written. Section 9.1 checks that `pivot_wider()` gives the same matrix.

The distances are in metres because SVY21 is a projected system. Dividing by 1000 gives kilometres.

```{r}
distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat/1000)
```

Because rows and columns carry no IDs now, the order has to line up with the sf objects. Rows should follow `hexagons$fid` and columns should follow `eldercare$fid`.

```{r}
all.equal(as.numeric(hexagons$fid), as.numeric(sort(unique(ODMatrix$origin_id))))
all.equal(as.numeric(eldercare$fid), as.numeric(colnames(distmat)))
```

Both should return `TRUE`. If the second did not, `eldercare$capacity` would be paired with the wrong columns without any error message.

# 6. Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using the Hansen Method

## 6.1 Computing Hansen's accessibility

The accessibility itself comes from `ac()` of **SpatialAcc**. The package manual lists the arguments, and they are worth a read before running anything.

`data.frame()` stores the output as `acc_Hansen`.

```{r}
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "Hansen"))
```

The default column name is untidy, so I rename it to `accHansen`.

```{r}
colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
head(acc_Hansen)
```

Next the data table becomes a tibble.

```{r}
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
```

`bind_cols()` of dplyr then attaches it to the hexagons. The result, `hexagon_Hansen`, stays a simple feature data frame.

```{r}
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```

```{r}
head(hexagon_Hansen)
```

The same steps fit in one chunk:

```{r}
#| eval: false
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```

::: callout-warning
### The one-chunk version used a different power

The reference's combined chunk has `power = 0.5`, while the step-by-step chunk above it uses `power = 2`. Both are presented as the same computation, and they are not. A lower power flattens the distance penalty, so the scores would be different. I set the combined chunk to `power = 2` to match what I actually ran. Section 9.2 compares the two powers directly.
:::

## 6.2 Visualising Hansen's accessibility

### 6.2.1 Extracting the map extent

`st_bbox()` of sf gives the extent of the `hexagons` layer, which keeps the map frame fixed across the three methods.

```{r}
mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)
```

The map layers hexagons coloured by `accHansen` under the eldercare points.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

## 6.3 Statistical graphic visualisation

The next comparison is the distribution of Hansen scores by planning region. `st_join()` adds the region field from `mpsz` to `hexagon_Hansen`.

```{r}
hexagon_Hansen <- st_join(hexagon_Hansen, mpsz,
                          join = st_intersects)
```

```{r}
nrow(hexagons)
nrow(hexagon_Hansen)
```

::: callout-warning
### More rows than hexagons

`st_intersects` matches every subzone a hexagon touches. A hexagon sitting across a subzone boundary gets one row per subzone, so `hexagon_Hansen` now has more rows than `hexagons`. Working from the shapefile geometry, I expect roughly 5,400 rows from 3,125 hexagons. Boundary hexagons are therefore counted more than once in each boxplot below. I kept the join as the reference has it. Section 9.3 redoes it with one region per hexagon.
:::

`ggplot()` draws the boxplot, with the mean marked in red. Scores are logged here, and only here.

```{r}
ggplot(data=hexagon_Hansen,
       aes(y = log(accHansen),
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary",
             fun="mean",
             colour ="red",
             size=2)
```

The reference passes `fun.y = "mean"`. ggplot2 renamed that argument to `fun` in version 3.3.0, and `fun.y` now raises a deprecation warning. I used `fun`. The plot is the same.

# 7. Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using the KD2SFCA Method

## 7.1 Computing KD2SFCA's accessibility

This section repeats the Hansen steps, with some of the code folded into one chunk. The `family` argument is now `"KD2SFCA"`, and `d0 = 5` is switched on.

```{r}
# distmat_km is in kilometres, so d0 = 5 means a 5 km catchment
acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            d0 = 5,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "KD2SFCA"))

colnames(acc_KD2SFCA) <- "accKD2SFCA"
acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)
```

With a 5 km catchment, some hexagons may have no centre inside it. Two counts to compare:

```{r}
sum(apply(distmat_km, 1, min) > 5)
sum(hexagon_KD2SFCA$accKD2SFCA == 0)
```

The first counts hexagons whose nearest centre is farther than 5 km. The second counts hexagons that scored zero. If `d0` works as a hard cut-off, the two numbers should match. From the csv, the first count should land near 1,281 of the 3,125 hexagons.

## 7.2 Visualising KD2SFCA's accessibility

`mapex` is reused for the `bbox` argument.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
tm_shape(hexagon_KD2SFCA,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accKD2SFCA",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: KD2SFCA method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

::: callout-note
If zeros make up a large share of these scores, several of the ten quantile breaks land on 0. A legend with fewer than ten classes would come from that and would not signal a mistake in the map code.
:::

## 7.3 Statistical graphic visualisation

The same region comparison, starting with the join.

```{r}
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- st_join(hexagon_KD2SFCA, mpsz,
                          join = st_intersects)
```

```{r}
ggplot(data=hexagon_KD2SFCA,
       aes(y = accKD2SFCA,
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary",
             fun="mean",
             colour ="red",
             size=2)
```

# 8. Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using the Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM) Method

## 8.1 Computing SAM accessibility

Same pattern again, with `family = "SAM"`.

```{r}
acc_SAM <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                         eldercare$capacity,
                         distmat_km,
                         d0 = 5,
                         power = 2,
                         family = "SAM"))

colnames(acc_SAM) <- "accSAM"
acc_SAM <- as_tibble(acc_SAM)
hexagon_SAM <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_SAM)
```

```{r}
sum(hexagon_SAM$accSAM == 0)
```

## 8.2 Visualising SAM's accessibility

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
tm_shape(hexagon_SAM,
         bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "accSAM",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: SAM method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

## 8.3 Statistical graphic visualisation

```{r}
hexagon_SAM <- st_join(hexagon_SAM, mpsz,
                       join = st_intersects)
```

```{r}
ggplot(data=hexagon_SAM,
       aes(y = accSAM,
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary",
             fun="mean",
             colour ="red",
             size=2)
```

# 9. Extras

Some extras I am documenting for exploration of this topic.

## 9.1 Does `pivot_wider()` give the same matrix as `spread()`?

The reference points to `pivot_wider()` as the modern replacement but never runs it. Here it is on the same three columns.

```{r}
distmat_pw <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = destination_id,
              values_from = total_cost) %>%
  select(-origin_id)

all.equal(as.matrix(distmat_pw), as.matrix(distmat))
```

::: callout-tip
### Why I wanted to explore this

`spread()` sorts the new columns by destination id. `pivot_wider()` orders them by first appearance in the data. They agree only if every origin lists destinations in ascending order, so a `TRUE` here is a fact about this csv. `all.equal()` compares column names too, so a different order would show up as a difference.
:::

## 9.2 How much does the Hansen power matter?

The reference runs power 2 in one place and 0.5 in another. Running three powers side by side shows how much that choice changes things.

```{r}
acc_pow <- sapply(c(0.5, 1, 2),
                  function(p) ac(hexagons$demand,
                                 eldercare$capacity,
                                 distmat_km,
                                 power = p,
                                 family = "Hansen"))
colnames(acc_pow) <- c("power_0.5", "power_1", "power_2")
summary(acc_pow)
```

```{r}
cor(acc_pow, method = "spearman")
```

The summary shows how the scale of the scores moves with the power. The rank correlation shows whether the map ordering moves with it. Those are two separate questions, and a high correlation with very different summaries is a possible outcome.

The Hansen chunk also carries a commented-out `d0 = 50`. A direct test of whether `d0` does anything for this family:

```{r}
acc_d0 <- ac(hexagons$demand,
             eldercare$capacity,
             distmat_km,
             d0 = 5,
             power = 2,
             family = "Hansen")

all.equal(as.numeric(acc_d0), as.numeric(acc_pow[, "power_2"]))
```

`TRUE` means Hansen ignores `d0`, which would fit why the reference leaves it commented out.

## 9.3 One region per hexagon

Section 6.3 duplicated boundary hexagons. `largest = TRUE` in `st_join()` keeps only the subzone with the biggest overlap, so each hexagon appears once.

```{r}
hexagon_Hansen_1 <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen) %>%
  st_join(mpsz %>% select(REGION_N),
          join = st_intersects,
          largest = TRUE)

nrow(hexagon_Hansen_1)
```

```{r}
table(hexagon_Hansen$REGION_N)
table(hexagon_Hansen_1$REGION_N)
```

The first table is the duplicated version. The second sums to 3,125.

```{r}
ggplot(data=hexagon_Hansen_1,
       aes(y = log(accHansen),
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary",
             fun="mean",
             colour ="red",
             size=2)
```

::: callout-tip
### Why I wanted to explore this

The reference boxplots count a hexagon once for every subzone it touches. Whether that visibly changes the picture depends on how much the extra rows differ from the rest of the region. Comparing this plot with the one in 6.3 shows how much the duplicates mattered.
:::

## 9.4 How sensitive is the zero share to `d0`, and do the methods agree?

Section 7.1 hinted that `d0 = 5` leaves many hexagons with nothing in reach. Trying three catchment sizes with the SAM family:

```{r}
d0_grid <- c(2, 5, 10)

zero_share <- sapply(d0_grid, function(d) {
  mean(ac(hexagons$demand,
          eldercare$capacity,
          distmat_km,
          d0 = d,
          power = 2,
          family = "SAM") == 0)
})
names(zero_share) <- paste0("d0_", d0_grid)
round(zero_share, 3)
```

The share of zeros should fall as the catchment widens, and the rate of that fall says how much of the island sits in the 5 to 10 km band. On method agreement, the three score vectors are aligned with `hexagons`, so they can be correlated directly.

```{r}
method_scores <- tibble(Hansen = acc_Hansen$accHansen,
                        KD2SFCA = acc_KD2SFCA$accKD2SFCA,
                        SAM = acc_SAM$accSAM)

cor(method_scores, method = "spearman")
```

Spearman is the safer choice here because zeros create many ties.

## 9.5 Putting `ggstatsplot` to use

A nonparametric comparison of logged Hansen scores across regions, using the one-row-per-hexagon data from 9.3:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
hexagon_Hansen_1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(log_acc = log(accHansen)) %>%
  ggbetweenstats(x = REGION_N,
                 y = log_acc,
                 type = "nonparametric",
                 pairwise.display = "none")
```

::: callout-tip
### Why I wanted to explore this

The boxplots in the reference only invite an eyeball comparison. This adds a test statistic and an effect size. Neighbouring hexagons are spatially autocorrelated, so the p-value is optimistic. I read it as a rough signal, and the effect size as the part to take away.
:::

# Summary of Adjustments

| Location in reference | Issue found | Correction applied |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| 17.4.2 (CRS check) | Only `mpsz` is checked after the transform | Added an EPSG check across all three layers before and after the transform |
| 17.4.3 and 17.5.2 (IDs and order) | `ac()` matches by position, but `eldercare$fid` has gaps (120 centres, ids up to 133) | Added checks that `hexagons$fid` and `eldercare$fid` line up with the matrix rows and columns |
| 17.5.2 (`spread()`) | Retired in tidyr in favour of `pivot_wider()` | Kept `spread()` as written, tested `pivot_wider()` in 9.1 |
| 17.6.1 (one-chunk Hansen) | `power = 0.5` differs from the `power = 2` used in the step-by-step version | Set to `power = 2` so both match, compared powers in 9.2 |
| Boxplot chunks (17.6.3, 17.7.3, 17.8.3) | `fun.y` is deprecated in ggplot2 | Changed to `fun` |
| `st_join()` before the boxplots | One row per touching subzone, so boundary hexagons repeat | Kept as in the reference, added a row count check, redone with `largest = TRUE` in 9.3 |
| 17.7.2 and 17.8.2 (quantile classes) | Many zero scores can collapse quantile breaks | Kept the reference code, added zero counts in 7.1 and 8.1 and a note in 7.2 |
